Dixon |title=Australian Languages: Their Nature and Development |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2002 |url=http://www.cambridge.org/catalogue/catalogue.asp?isbn=0521473780|page=xxxv}} | iso3 = xbg | aiatsis = S13 | glotto = bung1264 | glottorefname = Bunganditj | revived = by 2017 }} '''Bungandidj''' is a language of [[Australia]], spoken by the [[Bungandidj people]], [[Indigenous Australian]]s who lived in an area which is now in south-eastern [[South Australia]] and in south-western [[Victoria, Australia|Victoria]]. According to [[Christina Smith (teacher and missionary)|Christina Smith]] and her book on the Buandig people, the Bungandidj called their language ''drualat-ngolonung'' (speech of man), or ''Booandik-ngolo'' (speech of the Booandik).Christina Smith, ''[https://archive.org/details/booandiktribeso00smitgoog The Booandik Tribe of South Australian Aborigines: A Sketch of Their Habits, Customs, Legends, and Language]'', Spiller, 1880 As of 2017, there is a revival and maintenance programme under way for the language.{{cite book|title=Colonialism and its aftermath: A history of Aboriginal South Australia|editor1-last=Brock|editor1-first=Peggy|editor2-first=Tom|editor2-last=Gara|chapter=1. Structures of Aboriginal life at the time of colonisation in South Australia|first=Paul|last=Monaghan|page=17|publisher=Wakefield|date=2017|isbn=9781743054994|chapter-url=https://www.wakefieldpress.com.au/files/extracts/Colonialism_and_its_Aftermath_extract.pdf|others=Extract, pp.i-xxiii}} Historical variants of the name include: ''Bunganditj'', ''Bungandaetch'', ''Bunga(n)daetcha'', ''Bungandity'', ''Bungandit'', ''Buganditch'', ''Bungaditj'', ''Pungantitj'', ''Pungatitj'', ''Booganitch'', ''Buanditj'', ''Buandik'', ''Booandik'', ''Boandiks'', ''Bangandidj'', ''Bungandidjk'', ''Pungandik'', ''Bak-on-date'', ''Barconedeet'', ''Booandik-ngolo'', ''Borandikngolo'', ''Bunganditjngolo'', and ''Burhwundeirtch.'' == Phonology == Bungandidj phonology is typical of Australian languages generally, sharing characteristics such as a single series of stops (no voicing contrast) at six places of articulation, a full corresponding set of nasals, laminals at all four coronal places of articulation and two glides.{{Cite book|title=The Bunganditj (Buwandik) language of the Mount Gambier region|last=Blake|first=Barry J.|date=2003|publisher=Pacific Linguistics, Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University|others=Australian National University. Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies.|isbn=9780858834958|location=Canberra|oclc=56054287}} Extrapolating from historical written sources and knowledge of surrounding languages, Blake posits the following consonant inventory: === Consonants === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" ! rowspan="2" | ! colspan="2" |[[Peripheral consonant|Peripheral]] ! colspan="2" |[[Laminal consonant|Laminal]] ! colspan="2" |[[Apical consonant|Apical]] |- ![[Bilabial consonant|Bilabial]] ![[Velar consonant|Velar]] ![[Dental consonant|Dental]] ![[Palatal consonant|Palatal]] ![[Alveolar consonant|Alveolar]] ![[Retroflex consonant|Retroflex]] |- ![[Plosive]] |'''p''' {{IPAblink|p}} |'''k''' {{IPAblink|k}} |'''th''' {{IPAblink|t̪}} |'''tj''' {{IPAblink|c}} |'''t''' {{IPAblink|t}} |'''rt''' {{IPAblink|ʈ}} |- ![[Nasal consonant|Nasal]] |'''m''' {{IPAblink|m}} |'''ng''' {{IPAblink|ŋ}} |'''nh''' {{IPAblink|n̪}} |'''ny''' {{IPAblink|ɲ}} |'''n''' {{IPAblink|n}} |'''rn''' {{IPAblink|ɳ}} |- ![[Flap consonant|Flap]]/[[Trill consonant|Trill]] | colspan="2" | | | |'''rr''' {{IPAblink|r}} | |- ![[Lateral consonant|Lateral]] | colspan="2" | |'''lh''' {{IPAblink|l̪}} |'''ly''' {{IPAblink|ʎ}} |'''l''' {{IPAblink|l}} |'''rl''' {{IPAblink|ɭ}} |- ![[Approximant consonant|Approximant]] | colspan="2" |'''w''' {{IPAblink|w}} | |'''y''' {{IPAblink|j}} | |'''r''' {{IPAblink|ɻ}} |} === Vowels === {| class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" ! ![[Front vowel|Front]] ![[Central vowel|Central]] ![[Back vowel|Back]] |- ![[Close vowel|Close]] |'''i''' {{IPAblink|i}} | |'''u''' {{IPAblink|u}} |- ![[Open vowel|Open]] | |'''a''' {{IPAblink|a}} | |} === Notes on orthography === * Early descriptions of Bungandidj made no distinction between the trill/flap {{IPAslink|r}} and approximant {{IPAslink|ɻ}} and evidence for this contrast is based on comparative evidence only. Blake transcribes both as {{angbr|r}}. * Although there is no voicing distinction, stops are transcribed with voiced symbols {{angbr|b, g, dh, d, rd}} in homorganic nasal-stop clusters (where voicing is expected). * Syllable-final palatals are transcribed with the digraphs {{angbr|yt, yn, yl}} to avoid a final -y being confused with a vowel. * Historical sources include five vowel graphemes including {{angbr|e}} and {{angbr|o}}; however, it is likely that {{angbr|e}} belongs to the {{IPAslink|i}} phoneme and {{angbr|o}} belongs to the {{IPAslink|u}} phoneme. However, Blake conservatively retains some {{angbr|e}} and {{angbr|o}} segments where they are consistently transcribed in this way across historical sources. ==A poem== Smith (1880), on pages 138–139, records a poem written in Bungandidj : {{Transliteration|xbg|yul-yul, thumbal}} (Fly beetle, bat, night) {{Transliteration|xbg|kallaball, moonarerebul}} (Fly, march-fly, beetle) {{Transliteration|xbg|nana nan molanin}} (parrot, little parrot.) {{Transliteration|xbg|korotaa, king nal}} ([[Wattlebird|wattle bird]],) {{Transliteration|xbg|yongo birrit.}} ([[Noisy miner|minah bird]].) == References == {{reflist}} {{Pama–Nyungan languages|South}} {{Australian Aboriginal languages}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Drual languages]] [[Category:Extinct languages of South Australia]] [[Category:Extinct languages of Victoria (state)]]
